Disney Signed Zach King to Make Ten Shorts With Its Characters and Put His Star Wars Fan Film on Disney+
King will make 10 Illusion Shorts exclusively for Disney, build illusions around Hexed and Star Wars, and his hour-long cardboard Star Wars tribute, Cardboard Wars, debuts on Disney+; the fee was not disclosed.
Disney and creator Zach King, CEO of King Studio, with more than 185 million followers across platforms, announced a partnership on Nov. 18. King will make 10 original Illusion Shorts exclusively for Disney to distribute, including on Disney+, plus illusions built around Hexed, Star Wars and Disney parks for Disney+ and his own channels, and behind-the-scenes videos for Disney's social accounts. Disney+ also gets Cardboard Wars, his hour-long 2026 tribute to the 1977 Star Wars made with cardboard sets and costumes. Terms were not disclosed. Disney signed Dude Perfect to a company-wide creative partnership on Oct. 15.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): King's own Star Wars fan film is now a Disney+ title and his next ten shorts use Disney characters, so the license fee and who owns those shorts decide what a creator keeps from a studio partnership.
The Facts
  • Announced: Nov. 18, 2026, by The Walt Disney Company and Zach King. Fee not disclosed.
  • Scope: 10 original Illusion Shorts made exclusively for Disney to distribute, including on Disney+; new illusion content inspired by Hexed, Star Wars and other Disney films and experiences, for Disney+ and King's own channels; behind-the-scenes content for Disney social platforms.
  • Disney+ debut: Cardboard Wars, King's 2026 hour-long tribute to the original 1977 Star Wars, with cardboard sets, props and costumes.
  • King: CEO of King Studio; more than 185 million followers across platforms.
  • Quote, Asad Ayaz, Chief Marketing and Brand Officer, Disney: "We want to build lasting relationships with creators like Zach, giving their ideas room to grow across Disney."
  • Disney calls it the most extensive collaboration with King to date. Prior Disney creator deal: Dude Perfect, company-wide creative partnership, Oct. 15, 2026.
  • The Ankler (Nov. 19): the shorts are themed with Disney IP, including this month's Hexed.

Meta Is Selling 3D Movies on Quest Headsets for $16.99 and Has Billie Eilish's Tour Film Exclusive
More than 150 films, including Avatar and Deadpool & Wolverine, sell for $16.99 or rent for $6.99 in 3D; Meta says thousands more arrive with its $1,299 VR Glasses in spring 2027.
Meta launched more than 150 3D movies to rent or buy in the TV app on its Quest 3 and 3S headsets on Nov. 19, in the U.S. first. Titles include Avatar, Deadpool & Wolverine and Wicked: For Good; most cost $16.99 to buy and $6.99 to rent. Billie Eilish's concert film Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour, co-directed with James Cameron, is exclusive to Quest in 3D through Dec. 31. Meta says the library will reach thousands of titles, with international availability, when its $1,299 VR Glasses launch in spring 2027.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Avatar and Wicked: For Good are being sold again as 3D purchases on a headset, and whether a contract counts that sale as home video or as a new license decides what profit participants on those films collect.
The Facts
  • Launch: Nov. 19, 2026; TV app on Meta Quest 3 and 3S; U.S. only at first.
  • Library: more than 150 3D movies to rent or buy. Named titles: Deadpool & Wolverine, Avatar, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Jurassic World Rebirth, Wicked: For Good, Billie Eilish's Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour.
  • Price: most titles $16.99 to buy, $6.99 to rent; pricing varies.
  • Exclusive: Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (co-directed by Billie Eilish and James Cameron) available to buy and rent in 3D only on Meta Quest through Dec. 31.
  • Next: "thousands of titles" and international availability with Meta VR Glasses, spring 2027, $1,299 each.
  • Existing: Quest users already stream via YouTube, Prime Video and Disney+ (select 3D titles) apps, and Netflix or Apple TV through the browser.
  • Prior filing: on Nov. 17 this feed reported Meta converting Hollywood films to 3D with DNEG, starting with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

Kevin Mayer Says Media Mergers Will Run for Years Because Revenue Has Stopped Growing
At Doha Industry Days the Candle Media founder said NBCUniversal's splits are built to end in mergers, and that Candle sold Hello Sunshine because its live-action business fell short.
Candle Media founder Kevin Mayer, who ran Disney's Fox purchase as chief strategy officer, said at Doha Industry Days that "revenue isn't continuing to grow the way it was 10 years ago," and that this pushes companies to combine. He cited Skydance's merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. and said NBCUniversal's separation from Comcast and its split between cable networks and the studio and streaming business "are intended to ultimately lead to consolidation" with other companies, over "the next several years." He said Candle's Moonbug (CoComelon) has worked, while Hello Sunshine and other live-action assets fell short and were sold.
Potential Talent Implication: Mayer expects several more years of mergers, which means fewer separate buyers for films and series, and his own company kept CoComelon while selling Hello Sunshine, the star-founded label, because its live-action business missed its targets.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Kevin Mayer, founder of Candle Media; former Disney chief strategy officer (Fox, Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, BAMTech acquisitions).
  • Venue: keynote, Doha Industry Days (Doha Film Festival, Nov. 19 to 21, 2026).
  • Quote: "Revenue isn't continuing to grow the way it was 10 years ago. That usually indicates that most ecosystems need to consolidate."
  • Quote on NBCUniversal: the splits from Comcast and between cable networks and the rest "are intended to ultimately lead to consolidation of those two companies with other companies."
  • Quote: "when growth slows, you want to take that revenue base and amortize it over a smaller cost base." Expects an "ongoing process for the next several years."
  • On integration: Disney kept Pixar and Marvel creatively separate; "sometimes not integrating on the creative side, that's crucial."
  • Candle: Moonbug (CoComelon) "very successful"; CoComelon passed 200 million YouTube subscribers. Hello Sunshine sold back to Reese Witherspoon: "we gave it a really good shot ... Those worked ok, but they didn't workout to be up to sort of what we wanted to. So we recently sold those."
  • Prior filings: Hello Sunshine buyback reported Oct. 13, Oct. 16, Oct. 22 and Oct. 30 in this feed.

Imax Signed Its Biggest UK Deal With a Cinema Chain the Former Cineworld CEO Just Bought
Mooky Greidinger acquired Showcase Cinemas UK and agreed to install 13 Imax with Laser systems at 12 UK sites and one in Europe; five open in 2027.
Imax announced its largest UK deal: 13 Imax with Laser systems across 12 Showcase Cinemas locations in the UK and one more in Europe, five of them opening in 2027. The statement also disclosed that Mooky Greidinger, who left Cineworld in 2023 after its Chapter 11 restructuring, has acquired Showcase Cinemas UK. Imax CEO Rich Gelfond called the UK one of the company's most successful markets and said Imax is having its best year ever at the global box office. Imax promoted Giovanni Dolci to the new role of chief operating officer earlier this week.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Imax is adding 13 UK screens after its best year, and the release commitments and bonuses tied to premium-format screen counts may carry more weight for UK openings from 2027.
The Facts
  • Deal: 13 new Imax with Laser systems; 12 Showcase Cinemas UK locations plus one additional European location. Imax's largest UK deal.
  • Timing: five new UK Imax locations open in 2027; the rest over the next few years.
  • Ownership: Mooky Greidinger has acquired Showcase Cinemas UK (disclosed in Imax's statement). Greidinger left Cineworld in 2023 after its U.S. Chapter 11 process.
  • Rich Gelfond, Imax CEO: the agreement "significantly expands our footprint in one of our most successful markets"; Imax is delivering "our best year ever at the global box office."
  • Greidinger: Imax "plays a significant role in the results of the industry."
  • Imax management: Giovanni Dolci promoted to newly created chief operating officer, overseeing the global theater network (announced earlier the same week).
  • Corroboration: Variety (Former Cineworld CEO Mooky Greidinger Leads Acquisition of Showcase Cinemas in U.K.), THR (Imax Inks Largest Cinema Deal In U.K.), Screen International.

Andrea Scrosati, Who Took Fremantle Into Film With Poor Things, Is Leaving to Start His Own Company
Scrosati, group COO and CEO of continental Europe, led Fremantle's purchases of Element Pictures, Asacha Media Group and Lux Vide and stays until the end of January 2027.
Andrea Scrosati, Fremantle's group COO and CEO of continental Europe, is leaving after eight years to start a new venture, staying until the end of January 2027. Since joining from Sky Italia in late 2018 he ran the M&A drive that bought Element Pictures, Asacha Media Group and Lux Vide, and the labels made Fremantle a film backer: Poor Things, Priscilla, The Hand of God, Maria, Bugonia and Queer, with four Oscars from 17 nominations and a Golden Lion. He also launched Fremantle Documentaries and Sports and the AI-focused Imaginae Studios. He did not describe the new venture.
Potential Talent Implication: Fremantle's auteur film run came through the production companies Scrosati bought, and with him leaving, filmmakers working through Element Pictures and its sister labels may find out whether Fremantle keeps funding film at the same level.
The Facts
  • Who: Andrea Scrosati, Group COO and CEO of continental Europe, Fremantle (RTL Group / Bertelsmann). Joined late 2018 from Sky Italia.
  • Exit: leaving after eight years to launch a new entrepreneurial venture; remains until end of January 2027. Venture not described.
  • M&A he oversaw: Element Pictures, Asacha Media Group, Lux Vide.
  • Fremantle-backed films during his tenure: Poor Things, Priscilla, The Hand of God, Maria, Bugonia, Queer. Four Oscars from 17 nominations; Golden Lion (Venice).
  • Other builds: Fremantle Documentaries, Fremantle Sports, FAST channel business, AI-focused Imaginae Studios.
  • Quote, Jennifer Mullin, Fremantle Global CEO: "He has been instrumental in our growth and transformation, from helping build Fremantle into a true portfolio company and leading our M&A strategy, to establishing our film strategy."
  • Quote, Scrosati: "The time feels right for me to take the next step and focus on building something new."
  • Corroboration: THR (Andrea Scrosati to Leave Fremantle Group), Deadline (Fremantle Group COO Andrea Scrosati Exiting After Eight Years), Screen International.

Utopia's Distribution Chief Is Leaving to Help Filmmakers Release Their Own Films
Kyle Greenberg, who ran marketing and distribution on more than 100 Utopia films and booked Megalopolis with Francis Ford Coppola, is starting Greenhouse, a consultancy for self-distribution, after year end.
Kyle Greenberg, Utopia's longtime head of marketing and distribution, leaves at year end to launch Greenhouse, a consulting startup that builds release strategies for filmmakers, artists, labels and brands distributing their own work, which Deadline says more producers are turning to as indie distribution narrows. At Utopia, founded in 2018 by Robert Schwartzman and Cole Harper, he oversaw creative, publicity, theatrical, home video and streaming on more than 100 films and worked with Francis Ford Coppola to market and book Megalopolis. He will also expand his production label, Stupid Co, with Anna Maguire.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Filmmakers who release their own films keep the rights a distributor would otherwise hold, and the executive who ran releases on more than 100 Utopia titles is now selling that release work to them directly.
The Facts
  • Who: Kyle Greenberg, head of marketing and distribution, Utopia (co-founded 2018 by Robert Schwartzman and Cole Harper). Leaves at year end.
  • New venture: Greenhouse, a consulting startup developing "highly curated, hands-on release strategies" for filmmakers, artists, labels and brands supporting their own self-distribution.
  • Context (Deadline): an increasing number of producers are turning to self-distribution given challenges in the indie film market.
  • Track record: creative, publicity, marketing, theatrical, home video, physical media and streaming for more than 100 films; Utopia's service-based Circle Collective division. Films include Shiva Baby (Emma Seligman), We're All Going to the World's Fair (Jane Schoenbrun), Sick of Myself (Kristoffer Borgli), The Sweet East, Vortex (Gaspar Noe), Holy Spider (Ali Abbasi). Marketed and booked Megalopolis with Francis Ford Coppola; worked with Mike Figgis on Megadoc.
  • Quote: "While so many people in the industry are lamenting a lack of reliable distribution methods, Greenhouse will be an extension of the ethos that has served as the foundation of my career," which he calls "growth through disruption."
  • Also: scaling production label Stupid Co (founded 2024 with Anna Maguire); their feature Galicia! releases in 2027.

Netflix Is Paying Dan Lin About $15 Million to Leave, and Its TV Buyers Are Moving to Amazon
Two sources told Puck that Netflix is paying film head Dan Lin about $15 million in severance, while global TV head Peter Friedlander and several of his buyers have moved to Amazon.
Netflix shares have fallen 47 percent in a year, about $200 billion of market value, and engagement on its originals is down 3 percent this year per Luminate, Matthew Belloni reports from this week's executive retreat, where Bela Bajaria's replacement Peter Rice spoke for the first time. Under a severance policy of a year's salary plus benefits, Lin's exit costs about $15 million and deputy Doug Belgrad's high seven figures, two sources said; Netflix declined to comment. Friedlander, comedy executive Andy Weil, Mandy Schaffer with a business affairs group, and documentary chief Liz Franco now work at Amazon.
Potential Talent Implication: Many of the executives who bought Netflix's series, along with a business affairs group that negotiated with producers, now buy for Amazon, so a producer's Netflix relationships may now open doors at a second buyer.
The Facts
  • Market value: Netflix stock down 47 percent over the past year, roughly $200 billion of market value lost (Puck).
  • Engagement on Netflix originals down 3 percent so far this year, per Luminate.
  • Retreat: annual Netflix executive retreat at Casa Del Mar, Santa Monica, this week; vice presidents and above; Peter Rice spoke to the group for the first time; Ari Emanuel was a guest speaker.
  • Exits: content chief Bela Bajaria (fired last month), film head Dan Lin, deputy Doug Belgrad.
  • Severance (two sources; Netflix declined to comment): policy of one year's salary plus other benefits for VP level and above; about $15 million to Lin, high seven figures to Belgrad, more than both to Bajaria.
  • Moves to Amazon: global TV head Peter Friedlander; comedy TV executive Andy Weil; Mandy Schaffer and a business affairs group; several production executives under Blair Fetter in worldbuilding TV; documentary chief Liz Franco.
  • Kira Goldberg, in the Netflix film group since 2018, left for Paramount despite a counteroffer from Rice.
  • Platform talks: Netflix is negotiating with Fox One and has looked at Peacock about carrying other services' programming (Puck).
  • Sarandos to Bloomberg this week: "We should be doing better in the U.S. than we were."
  • Paid subscribers: at least 325 million.
  • Belloni's own view: he expects Netflix to make an offer for all or part of NBCUniversal (analyst opinion, attributed).

Disney Is Reviving Home Alone for Theaters With Macaulay Culkin Back as Kevin
Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg closed a deal for their Point Grey company to produce and write the story with Culkin, who has not made a Home Alone film since 1992.
Disney has a Home Alone sequel or reboot in development with Macaulay Culkin, 46, returning as Kevin McCallister, Matthew Belloni reports in Puck. Rogen and Goldberg, whose Point Grey produced this year's Muppets reboot for Disney, closed their deal and will crack the script with Culkin after first prepping an original horror comedy they plan to direct for Universal, where they have a film first-look. Culkin met studio head David Greenbaum in July and brought his own idea for the movie. Disney inherited the property from Fox and has made only a direct-to-Disney+ sequel. Disney declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Disney owned Home Alone for years and made one streaming sequel, and the theatrical version moved only when the original star came back with his own idea, which may put a returning lead in a strong position on a dormant franchise.
The Facts
  • Project: Home Alone sequel/reboot, officially in development at Disney (Puck; Disney declined to comment).
  • Star: Macaulay Culkin, 46, returning as Kevin McCallister; last played the role on film in Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992); appeared as Kevin in a McDonald's ad this year.
  • Producers: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg via Point Grey; deal closed; will work with Culkin to crack a script.
  • Sequence: Rogen and Goldberg first prep an original horror comedy they plan to direct for Universal, where they have a first-look arrangement for movies.
  • July 2026: Culkin met Disney studio head David Greenbaum on the lot.
  • Franchise history at Disney: inherited from Fox; one direct-to-Disney+ sequel, officially the sixth Home Alone.
  • Streaming demand: the original returned to Nielsen's U.S. streaming movie top 10 this week at number nine, 177 million minutes on Disney+.

Trump Says the 20 Percent Federal Film Credit Will Pass and May Cover Live Theater
Asked how he would work with a Democratic Congress, Trump cited Adam Schiff's support for the incentive and said it will happen, though advocates still have no year-end bill to carry it.
President Trump told reporters Friday that the Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a 20% federal production incentive introduced in September by Sens. Tim Scott and Adam Schiff, has "unbelievable support" and is "going to happen," Deadline reports. He said live theatrical productions may be added. Deadline reports it is still unclear whether the bill can pass in the lame-duck session, where advocates want it attached to a year-end funding or tax package; Democrats take control of both chambers next year.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A presidential endorsement still does not put the credit in a year-end bill, so 2027 production budgets cannot count on it yet, and stage producers may now have a federal incentive to track alongside film and television.
The Facts
  • Bill: Motion Picture, Television and Entertainment Revitalization Act; 20% production incentive; introduced in the Senate and House in September by members of both parties (Sens. Tim Scott, R-SC, and Adam Schiff, D-CA, in the Senate).
  • Trump, Friday press conference: "It's running its way through Congress and it has unbelievable support." "I can tell you right now, it's going to happen."
  • Trump said live theatrical productions may be added to the incentive.
  • Trump on production flight: "We don't make movies in this country anymore, you know. They go to Canada, they go to UK, and they go to Australia."
  • Same day: Trump met Jon Voight, an incentive advocate, and posted on social media about passing it.
  • Status (Deadline): unclear whether it can pass in the lame-duck session; advocates hope to attach it to a year-end funding bill or tax package; Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress next year.
  • Industry trade groups and unions lobbied on Capitol Hill this past week.
  • Prior filing: 2026-11-19-01 (cosponsor count House 76, Senate 14). The Ankler (Nov. 20) counts 12 more senators and 68 House members signed on.

Hello Sunshine's Film and TV President Is Leaving a Month After Witherspoon Bought It Back
Lauren Neustadter, who produced Big Little Lies, The Morning Show and Where the Crawdads Sing, is leaving after the company cut half its staff following the Mediawan-backed buyback.
Lauren Neustadter, president of film and television at Reese Witherspoon's Hello Sunshine since shortly after its 2017 launch, is leaving, TheWrap, Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter report. Witherspoon and Mediawan bought the majority stake back from Candle Media just over a month ago for a low- to mid-eight-figure sum, TheWrap reports, against a $900 million valuation in 2021, and the company then cut 50% of its staff, about 30 people by Deadline's count. TheWrap and THR put her exit at year's end.
Potential Talent Implication: Projects set up at Hello Sunshine, including the third season of Big Little Lies and TriStar's The Nightingale, now go forward without the executive who developed them, inside a company running on half its staff and backed by Mediawan.
The Facts
  • Who: Lauren Neustadter, President of Film & Television, Hello Sunshine; joined shortly after the 2017 launch; previously SVP Programming at Fox, earlier film executive at Miramax and Twentieth Century Fox.
  • Timing: TheWrap and THR say end of year; Deadline says she works through the end of the day.
  • Ownership: Witherspoon and Mediawan bought back the majority stake from Candle Media (Kevin Mayer, Tom Staggs) for low- to mid-eight figures (TheWrap), versus a $900 million valuation when Candle acquired it in 2021.
  • Staff: cut 50% after the sale (TheWrap); about 30 employees (Deadline).
  • Credits: The Morning Show (heading into fifth and final season), Big Little Lies (returning for season three), Little Fires Everywhere, Elle, From Scratch, Lucky, Surface, The Last Thing He Told Me, Truth Be Told, Tiny Beautiful Things, Daisy Jones & The Six; films Something from Tiffany's, Your Place or Mine, You're Cordially Invited, Where the Crawdads Sing, and TriStar's upcoming The Nightingale.
  • Mediawan: produces more than 450 titles a year through nearly 100 labels in 15 countries, including Chernin Entertainment, Plan B, See-Saw Films and The North Road Company.
  • Neustadter: "Building Hello Sunshine alongside Reese and our incredible team has been the privilege of a lifetime."
  • Witherspoon: "Lauren's taste, passion, and leadership have been integral to Hello Sunshine's film and television success."
  • Prior filings: 2026-10-13-09 (buyback), 2026-10-22-01 (sale price), 2026-10-30-11 (staff cut).

Most SAG-AFTRA Members Do Not Earn Enough to Qualify for the Union Health Plan
President Sean Astin said a substantial majority of members miss the $28,090 earnings or 108-day work threshold, and the board voted Friday to form a task force pushing universal health care.
SAG-AFTRA's national board voted unanimously Friday to create a President's Healthcare Task Force to advocate for universal health care, The Hollywood Reporter reports. Astin said the health plan is financially sound but most members do not qualify, because they earn under $28,090 or work fewer than 108 days a year. Under terms negotiated with studios and streamers this year, eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold rise slightly in 2027, with more increases after. Since Nov. 1 the union has again terminated members behind on dues, and thousands have been dropped, according to Variety.
Potential Talent Implication: Health coverage for most working actors depends on reaching $28,090 or 108 days in a slow production year, and the threshold rises in 2027, so a single booking can decide whether an actor is insured.
The Facts
  • Board action (Friday, Nov. 20): unanimous vote to create the President's Healthcare Task Force, a public-policy group to advocate for universal health care.
  • Eligibility: $28,090 minimum annual earnings or 108 applicable days of work per year.
  • Astin: the SAG-AFTRA Health Plan is on strong financial footing, but a substantial majority of members do not qualify.
  • 2027: eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold rise slightly under this year's contract with studios and streamers, with further increases in later years.
  • Dues: as of Nov. 1 the union resumed terminating memberships of members who owe dues; thousands dropped (Variety, via THR).
  • Pressure: Cheyenne Jackson's "One Job Away" campaign (late October) on actors one or a few jobs short of coverage.
  • Union leadership: board extended Duncan Crabtree-Ireland's contract to 2032 on Oct. 24, reportedly with a 15 percent raise; prior published gross salary $1,068,535.

Newsmax says Fox's Tubi and The Roku Channel together hold about 71% of U.S. viewing time in free ad-supported streaming, enough to limit rival networks' reach.
Newsmax filed a federal antitrust suit in California on Wednesday seeking to unwind Fox Corp.'s $22 billion acquisition of Roku, which closed Nov. 6 after the Justice Department ended its review, TheWrap reports. Newsmax distributes its Newsmax2 channel through The Roku Channel and says Fox could make it harder for rival networks to get favorable placement.   • Target: Fox Corp.'s $22 billion acquisition of Roku, completed Nov. 6, 2026.

2026-11-17 Tuesday 14 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 10 opportunities · 4 challenges
Opportunities
  • Disney is adding money for content while it cuts staff, but the new dollars are aimed at international programming, sports and streaming engagement, so producers pitching Disney may find the open budget sits outside the domestic scripted slate.
  • A writer who created a franchise before the studio deal now holds a date the owner has to buy past, and under the Fifth Circuit ruling the price could cover worldwide rights, not only the United States. (Rights Ownership)
  • Packer took equity money from a studio he has made films for and kept the CEO seat, which gives a producer with a defined audience a template: a studio can be a co-investor in the producer's company rather than only the buyer of its projects. (Company Building)
  • Disney+ is now a buyer for creator video tied to its own franchises, which puts a value on creators who can make Marvel-adjacent content and raises the question, still unanswered in the release, of how those creators are paid and who owns what they make. (New Revenue Stream)
  • A brand that owns the show needs a producer and a face it trusts, so talent with their own production company can sell directly to marketers, though the reporting does not say who owns the format or how Hartbeat is paid. (New Revenue Stream)
  • A film recut with new immersive moments for a headset is a new version of the work, which raises whether the director approves it, as Francis Lawrence is involved here, and whether it counts as a new window under existing backend terms. (Project Economics)
  • Ayer is a managing partner in the company that rents the stage he plans to use, so a director who brings his own slate to a cheaper production method can own part of the savings. (Company Building)
  • Guild brought 96 million subscribers to the deal, so the studio works for a share of ad revenue while he keeps ownership of the character and the show. (Rights Ownership)
  • A creator's public view count now includes YouTube's estimate of people watching together on a TV, which raises the number brands and buyers see while the creator's ad revenue stays on the old count. (New Revenue Stream)
  • The bigger content budget is aimed at local-language series, sports and franchise films, so international producers gain a better-funded buyer while US talent should expect licensing-revenue definitions to matter more as Disney titles travel to rival platforms. (Project Economics)
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Paramount and Warner Bros. answer to the same two co-chairs, so a package shopped to both may draw one decision, while the 30-film commitment still requires the merged studio to fill its slate.
  • Banijay is growing in live events and sport while its production revenue shrinks, so creators selling formats or series to the merged company may find fewer production slots than an $8 billion merger suggests.
  • Unscripted and animation sellers who pitched the Paramount and WBD cable networks separately now face four programming chiefs across more than 50 channels, though the merged animation studios can still make shows for outside platforms.
  • Amazon's executive chairman took part in choosing Bond alongside Villeneuve, so approvals on that franchise reach the top of the company, a fact anyone negotiating casting or creative control on future Bond films now has on the record.
Disney Will Raise Content Spending to $26 Billion While Cutting $3 Billion in Costs
Disney guided fiscal 2027 cash content spend up about 9% to roughly $26 billion while targeting $3 billion in annual cost savings by fiscal 2029, mostly reinvested in streaming content, technology and marketing.
Disney reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue up 16% to $25.9 billion and adjusted EPS of $1.77, against $1.11 a year earlier. Disney+ and Hulu operating income more than doubled to $824 million. The company guided fiscal 2027 cash content spend to about $26 billion, including more international programming and sports rights, and set a $3 billion annual run-rate savings target by fiscal 2029 from labor, procurement, IT and real estate. CFO Hugh Johnston said most savings go back into streaming content, technology and marketing.
Potential Talent Implication: Disney is adding money for content while it cuts staff, but the new dollars are aimed at international programming, sports and streaming engagement, so producers pitching Disney may find the open budget sits outside the domestic scripted slate.
The Facts

  • Fiscal 2026 revenue: $102.3 billion, up 8% from $94.4 billion.
  • Q4 adjusted EPS: $1.77 vs. $1.11; diluted EPS $1.51 vs. $0.73.
  • Entertainment segment Q4: revenue $11.9 billion (up 17%); operating income $1,327 million vs. $691 million.
  • SVOD (Disney+ and Hulu) Q4 operating income: $824 million, up $422 million; full-year streaming operating margin 11.5% (TheWrap).

  • Release: "annual run-rate operating expense savings of approximately $3 billion by fiscal 2029."

  • Johnston declined to give the split between sports and entertainment spend (TheWrap).
  • Prior cuts in 2026 (TheWrap): 1,000 roles in April; hundreds in July incl. Pixar and National Geographic; a few hundred in technology and HR in September; 100 to 200 in parks in October.
  • Disney+ to roughly triple local original programming over three years; more than 30 partnerships with local free-to-air broadcasters (TheWrap).
  • SVOD operating income disclosure ends starting Q1 fiscal 2027; D'Amaro: "We no longer believe the supplemental disclosure of SVOD operating income reflects this segment focus and strategy."
  • Fiscal 2027 guidance: operating income growth about 8%; capex about $9 billion; free cash flow about $11 billion; buybacks about $9 billion. Investor Day set for May 2027.

The Wachowskis Have Served Notice to Take Back The Matrix From Warner Bros.
Lana and Lilly Wachowski formally notified Warner Bros. they are terminating its grant of The Matrix rights, effective as soon as February 2029, while Drew Goddard develops Matrix 5.
Puck's Eriq Gardner reports the Wachowskis served Warner Bros., now part of Skydance, a copyright termination notice (an author's statutory right to reclaim a rights grant after a waiting period). To keep making sequels past that date, Skydance would need a fresh grant. The studio could argue The Matrix was work made for hire, which cannot be terminated, though Warner Bros. said in an earlier lawsuit that the sisters wrote it before their 1994 deal. A Fifth Circuit ruling the Supreme Court let stand this summer allows termination to reach worldwide rights.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A writer who created a franchise before the studio deal now holds a date the owner has to buy past, and under the Fifth Circuit ruling the price could cover worldwide rights, not only the United States.
The Facts
  • Notice: Lana and Lilly Wachowski have formally notified Warner Bros. they are exercising copyright termination rights on The Matrix (Puck, "I've learned"; no named source).
  • Effective date: as soon as February 2029, in the U.S. "and maybe beyond."
  • Matrix 5 is in development with Drew Goddard shepherding; per Puck the sisters have encouraged it and recently increased their involvement. Lilly Wachowski said in September she does not want to "play in that sandbox anymore."
  • Origin: The Matrix was part of a three-picture deal folded together in 1994 (Assassins, Bound, The Matrix). In an earlier copyright lawsuit Warner Bros. appeared to contend the Wachowskis began The Matrix in 1992 and had drafted scripts for all three films by 1993.
  • Precedents (Puck): Skydance negotiated a new deal last year for The Godfather after Mario Puzo's estate exercised termination against Paramount; Annapurna bought The Terminator in 2011 knowing U.S. rights reverted in 2019, and Skydance later dealt with James Cameron.
  • Other terminations Skydance faces (Puck): The Shawshank Redemption, Beavis and Butt-Head, ER (Sherri Crichton, widow of Michael Crichton, is already contesting The Pitt on contract grounds).
  • Law: in BMG v. Vetter the Fifth Circuit held termination can reclaim rights worldwide; the Supreme Court lacked a quorum after four recusals and affirmed by default this summer.
  • Paramount's amicus brief (Lisa Blatt, Williams & Connolly) said worldwide termination would "encourage authors to seek extortionate prices from studios by threatening to sell all rights to make derivative works worldwide to the highest bidder," and called it an "existential threat to the practice of creating derivative works."
  • Disclosure (Puck): RedBird Capital, a Skydance investor, also invests in Puck.

YouTube View Counts Now Include People Watching Together on a TV

  • Scope: new TV views only; not retroactive.
  • Money: co-views do not affect a creator's ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility or revenue.

Disney Is Raising Content Spend 9 Percent to $26 Billion, With the New Money Going to Local-Language Series, Sports and Franchise Films
Disney beat on revenue and EPS in its fiscal fourth quarter, guided fiscal 2027 cash content spend up about 9 percent to $26 billion, and said it will stop reporting streaming operating income as a separate line from next quarter.
Disney reported fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $25.9 billion, up 15.5 percent, and adjusted EPS of $1.77 against $1.68 expected, with an extra 53rd week adding roughly 7 points of revenue growth [R] [2nd]. Streaming had its best quarter: SVOD revenue rose 19 percent to $6.05 billion and SVOD operating income doubled to $824 million [R]. For fiscal 2027 Disney guided cash content spend to about $26 billion, up about 9 percent, driven by sports rights, international programming and feature film production, and it plans to roughly triple local originals for Disney+ over three years [R]. From fiscal Q1 2027 it drops the SVOD operating income disclosure; CFO Hugh Johnston said the change gives "greater flexibility to manage the cost base of the entire portfolio" [R] [call]. A $3 billion efficiency program runs to fiscal 2029, mostly reinvested, and CEO Josh D'Amaro defended licensing Ice Age and Percy Jackson to Netflix on a co-exclusive basis as "additive" [R] [call]. DIS was up about 1.1 percent at midday [2nd].
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): The bigger content budget is aimed at local-language series, sports and franchise films, so international producers gain a better-funded buyer while US talent should expect licensing-revenue definitions to matter more as Disney titles travel to rival platforms.
The Facts
  • Q4 FY26 (14 weeks, ended 10/3/26): revenue $25,947M (+15.5%), total segment operating income $4,970M (+42.8%), adjusted EPS $1.77 vs $1.11 [R]; consensus $1.68 EPS and $25.17B revenue [2nd].
  • FY26: revenue $102.3B (+8.4%), adjusted EPS $7.02 (+18.4%); the 53rd week added about $1.6B of revenue and $0.17 of EPS [R].
  • Entertainment SVOD: revenue $6,050M (+19.1%), operating income $824M vs $402M; FY26 SVOD margin 11.5% [R].
  • FY27 guide: double-digit adjusted EPS growth ex-53rd week, segment OI up about 8%, cash content spend about $26B (+9%), capex about $9B, buybacks about $9B; dividend raised 33% to $2.00 [R].
  • About $3B in annual run-rate savings by FY2029, mostly reinvested; FY26 restructuring and impairment charges $1.46B [R].
  • Titles: Toy Story 5 20M Disney+ views in five days [R] and over $1B global box office [call]; The Devil Wears Prada 2 close to $700M worldwide [call]; The Remarried Empress biggest local original premiere to date [R].
  • Slate: Avengers: Doomsday 12/18, Hexed, Pixar's Gatto in March, Frozen 3 and Lilo & Stitch 2 in FY2028 [R].
  • ESPN holds exclusive rights to the 23-game College Football Playoff from 2027 and carries its first Super Bowl in February 2027 [R] [call].
  • Investor event on long-term strategy set for May 2027 [call].

UK Actors Would Be Paid Every Time a Digital Replica Is Used Under Equity's New Deal
Equity is recommending its 8,000 actors accept Pact's final offer: consent and payment for each use of a digital replica, a 24% raise on films over £50 million and streamer use fees up three points.
After nearly three years of talks, British actors union Equity is recommending members accept producer body Pact's final offer, Deadline reports. The deal covers most UK film and TV from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2029. Actors must consent to each use of a digital replica, project by project, and are paid when it is used; blanket consent is barred. Equity did not win a right to have replicas deleted. Streaming platform use fees (paid when a show gets a second window on a streamer) rise three percentage points, and the payment period falls from 15 years to 10.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A UK actor's digital replica now carries a fee and a consent right on every project, so a scan made for one production gives the producer nothing it can reuse on the next.
The Facts
  • Parties: Equity (UK actors union, about 8,000 actor members) and Pact (UK producer trade body). Final offer goes to a member vote with a "yes" recommendation, the first time members vote on this agreement.
  • Term: January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2029; covers actors on the majority of British film and TV.
  • AI provisions, four parts: digital replicas, digital alterations of a performance, "Synthetics," and obligations on AI training licensing.
  • Digital replicas: actors "have the right to be paid when your digital replica is used" and "the right to consent" with information on the specific use before consenting. A producer "cannot obtain blanket consent," only consent for specific projects. Substantive changes to scenes agreed in a nudity rider need the actor's approval.
  • Not won: contractual protections for replica deletion, and for digital scanning customarily used for CGI, VFX and SFX.
  • Pay: films budgeted over £50 million ($66 million) +24% over three years (17% in year one); films £30 million to £50 million +13% (7% in year one); TV +9% (3% a year).
  • Streaming platform use fees: +3 percentage points, which Equity says could be a real-terms rise of up to 50%; the period these apply over cut from 15 years to 10.
  • Self-tapes: producers must give 72 hours' notice when sending scripts.
  • Also new: bullying and harassment principles, and a Green Rider on sustainability.
  • Deadline understands the end of streamer "special stipulations" will likely be addressed in Equity's later talks with the US streamers.
  • Quote, Equity General Secretary Paul W Fleming: "We've achieved the best AI provisions in the business."

Apple Will Put Video Podcasts on TV Screens for Free and Charge Creators Nothing
Apple began developer testing on November 16 of a video podcast section in the Apple TV app, free without a subscription, on more than 1 billion devices including Roku players and smart TVs.
Apple will bring video shows from Apple Podcasts into the Apple TV app with no subscription required, The Hollywood Reporter and TheWrap report, following The New York Times; no launch date is set. Apple says the number of podcasts publishing video to its platform doubled in three months. Since February, creators can insert their own video ads, including host reads, and Apple has said it will not charge creators or hosting providers to distribute; ad networks pay impression-based fees.

  • Apple figures: podcasts publishing video to its platform doubled in the last three months; the video episode catalog tripled; top podcasts with video episodes saw a 20% viewing boost on average (THR).

Opportunities
  • Talent with overall deals, backend or franchise rights at NBCUniversal could face a different counterparty if Netflix ever buys it, and a streamer owning a studio and theme parks could price film, TV and park rights as one package. (Project Economics)

Challenges & Headwinds

  • Netflix executives want venues that promote shows and may earn a little money, which puts a Netflix House license nearer to marketing than to a revenue stream for the creators behind a franchise.

Michael Mann Is Using Copyright Termination to Reclaim Heat, and New Regency Has Sued
New Regency says Mann wrote Heat as a work for hire and cannot terminate, and its complaint says provisions in both sides' Heat 2 agreements with Amazon depend on the outcome.
Earlier this year Mann served New Regency three termination notices under the Copyright Act provision that lets authors reclaim rights they granted, covering the Heat screenplay and underlying materials, including an alleged 1988 oral agreement from Mann and two companies he controlled. New Regency sued Friday in California federal court to have the screenplay declared a work made for hire (the employer counts as author, and such works cannot be terminated). It says the notices cloud its title and impair its ability to develop, finance and license derivative works. Mann's spokesperson says Heat 2 starts shooting January 19, unaffected.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A writer-director who wrote a property on his own and assigned it later may be able to take it back, so for Heat and its sequels the 1988 paperwork, a work-for-hire commission or a later assignment, decides who owns the franchise.
The Facts
  • Filed: Friday, November 13, 2026, California federal court; New Regency Productions v. Michael Mann; declaratory relief that the Heat screenplay "is not subject to termination."
  • Mann's notices: three, served earlier in 2026; the first sought to terminate all copyright grants for Heat, including an alleged 1988 oral agreement from Mann and two companies he controlled.
  • Per the complaint, Mann told New Regency the assignment was never put in writing and that he only recently discovered the arrangement.
  • New Regency's argument: Mann wrote the screenplay as a work made for hire; works made for hire are generally not eligible for termination.
  • Complaint: "The Termination Notices cloud Regency's title to the Screenplay and impair its ability to develop, finance, and license works derived from it."
  • Complaint: "certain provisions of the agreements that Mann and Regency each entered into with Amazon with respect to Heat 2 depend on the outcome of this litigation."
  • Mann spokesperson: "After 40 years, Michael Mann is exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work"; "confident that the courts will vindicate Michael Mann's statutory rights under the Copyright Act."
  • Heat 2: based on Mann's 2022 novel; shooting begins January 19, 2027, per Mann's statement; the statement says the filing is unrelated to production.
  • Heat (1995): written, produced and directed by Mann.

Netflix's Share of U.S. Original-Series Viewing Fell to 58 Percent
Luminate counts 13 of Netflix's 25 most-streamed series above 5 billion minutes this year, down from 23 a year ago, and puts its share of original viewing at 58 percent.
A Luminate report by analyst Tyler Aquilina puts Netflix's share of U.S. original-series viewing time at 58 percent, down from more than two-thirds in 2024 and about 60 percent in 2025. Returning hits such as Bridgerton and The Lincoln Lawyer lost viewers in their fourth seasons, and five of Netflix's ten most-watched original seasons this year were limited series or final seasons. Aquilina said viewers are spreading their time across more platforms and that Netflix needs a title that connects at scale. New content chief Peter Rice inherits the problem; Netflix declined to comment.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Half of Netflix's ten most-watched originals this year will not return, which leaves a showrunner who can deliver a returning series at scale holding what Netflix most needs while its share of original viewing slips.

  • Netflix top 25 most-streamed series with more than 5 billion minutes: 13 this year vs 23 in the same period of 2025.

Most Film Editors in an Avid Survey Already Use AI, Mostly for Logging and Search
Of 120 American Cinema Editors members surveyed by Avid, 77.5 percent use AI in post, mainly for transcription, audio cleanup and shot search; 7.5 percent want it assembling rough cuts.
Avid, which sells the Media Composer editing software, surveyed 120 of the American Cinema Editors' 1,200 members. Transcription led at 60 percent, audio cleanup 55 percent and searching footage for specific shots 39.2 percent. Ethical, copyright and security concerns made up nearly half the barriers to use. Emmy-nominated editor Molly Shock said that on MasterChef, AI found a contestant's clock-check shot in seconds, and some half-day tasks now take 15 minutes; she said editors want a say in how the tools are used so the system does not remove "any kind of growth."
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Editors have adopted AI for media management faster than the industry admitted, and the open question for them is staffing and training on AI-assisted shows, where Shock's worry is the career ladder.
The Facts
  • Survey: Avid; 120 of ACE's 1,200 members; 77.5 percent use AI to some extent in post-production.
  • Uses: transcription 60 percent; audio cleanup 55 percent; shot search 39.2 percent; also generating reference shots and tagging.
  • Only 7.5 percent want AI to help assemble shots or rough cuts; nearly 100 percent of daily or weekly users say AI should only enhance the creative vision.
  • Barriers: ethical, copyright and security concerns, nearly 50 percent.
  • Matt Feury, Avid VP of artist relations: editors use AI "to minimize the amount of manual stuff... the media management, the metadata management."
  • Molly Shock (Emmy-nominated editor), on MasterChef: some days "half a day's work has been reduced to 15 minutes."
  • Shock: "You adapt or die. So that's a pretty big incentive."
  • Article cites InterPositive, Ben Affleck's company, now owned by Netflix, among tools in use across Hollywood.

The WGA Gave the 1999 Thomas Crown Writers Screenplay Credit on a Remake They Never Worked On
Kurt Wimmer and Leslie Dixon will share screenplay credit with Drew Pearce on Amazon MGM's Thomas Crown Affair, opening March 5, 2027, and Jason Hall, credited on the first trailer, could lose his.
The Writers Guild awarded screenplay credit on Michael B. Jordan's Thomas Crown Affair to Kurt Wimmer and Leslie Dixon, who wrote the 1999 version and did not work on the new film. Drew Pearce shares the credit. Alan Trustman, writer of the 1968 original, and Joe Carnahan, who wrote an earlier draft, get story credit. LightShed Puts YouTube's Price for Carrying Peacock at About $3 a Subscriber
LightShed estimates YouTube pays about $3 per subscriber a month for Peacock's ad tier inside YouTube Premium, more than 70% below retail, and lets NBCU sell the ads, a first for YouTube.
In a November 11 note, LightShed's Rich Greenfield, Brandon Ross and Mark Kelley argue streamers now either carry other services inside their own app or get carried by one. From early 2027 every U.S. YouTube Premium member gets Peacock's ad tier; LightShed estimates YouTube pays about $3 per subscriber a month, against Peacock's reported $8.40 subscription ARPU (average revenue per user), and says YouTube lets NBCU sell Peacock's ads and shares viewer data it has not given third parties before. Antenna estimated Amazon held at least 49 million channel subscriptions as of June 2026.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): When Peacock reaches tens of millions of new homes at about $3 a head (LightShed's estimate) instead of $8.40, a Peacock show's audience grows while subscription money per viewer falls, and backend tied to subscription revenue may be measured against the smaller number.
The Facts
  • Platform-wide ingestion (LightShed's term): the platform pays a wholesale fee and every member gets the carried service inside the platform's app. Examples: Netflix carrying TF1 in France (since June); Disney+ carrying Channel 4 in the U.K. (early 2027); YouTube Premium carrying Peacock in the U.S. (early 2027).
  • A la carte ingestion (channel stores): Prime Video Channels, Roku Premium Subscriptions, YouTube Primetime Channels; the platform's cut "can run upwards of 25%-30%."
  • LightShed estimate: YouTube pays around $3 per subscriber per month for Peacock's ad-supported tier, "a wholesale haircut of well over 70%" to retail and about a 50% discount to subscription ARPU.
  • NBCU reported Peacock subscription ARPU of $8.40 for Q3 2026 (blend of about 80% ad-tier, 20% ad-free).
  • Per LightShed: YouTube granted NBCU the right to sell ads inside Peacock on YouTube, the first time YouTube has let another company sell ads on its platform, and is providing viewer data it has not shared with third parties before.
  • Antenna: Amazon had at least 49 million channel subscriptions as of June 2026; one-third of new streaming subscriptions come through channel stores.
  • YouTube: 16% of TV time spent, the most-watched platform on TV (per LightShed).
  • Skydance: Ellison said on the Q3 call the company sees value in being "a predominantly direct business" but will decide distribution partnerships partner by partner, naming Amazon and Walmart.
  • Matt Strauss (NBCU Media Group chairman, Decoder podcast): "We need to be an open ecosystem... we're almost indifferent about where somebody consumes the content."

CAA Clients Can Now License AI Replicas for Ogilvy Ads Without a New Shoot
Ogilvy's ECHO platform will generate ads from CAA Vault scans of clients who opt in, with talent approving every asset; Ogilvy puts the cost saving per asset at 65 to 75 percent.
Ogilvy, part of WPP, and CAA announced the partnership Monday after a year of work. The CAA Vault, a 204-camera scanning studio Veritone built for CAA four years ago, captures a client's face, voice, body language and walk, refreshed every three to five years. ECHO pulls that material into WPP's production system. Terry Crews has opted in, and Ogilvy is negotiating pilots due near year-end. CAA says clients own their digital likenesses and choose which brands and markets they appear for. Every ad carries a "[Talent Name] Approved | Recreated with AI" watermark.

The Facts
  • Partners: Ogilvy (WPP) and CAA; product name ECHO; announced 2026-11-09; a year in the making (Ogilvy's Carol Reed).

  • Workflow: Vault material feeds WPP Open for storyboards, mock-ups and final assets. THR: a traditional shoot of 8 to 10 assets can be expanded to roughly 30 to 50.

  • Alex Shannon, CAA head of strategic development: "We built The CAA Vault to ensure that talent owns, controls, and can safely monetize their digital likeness on their own terms and only with their consent."

Elvis Presley's Rights Holders Are Suing Suno Under Tennessee's Voice-Cloning Law
Rights holders of Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records filed two suits against Suno, the Presley suit claiming a violation of Tennessee's ELVIS Act on AI voice cloning.
Both suits claim the AI music company generates music and lyrics that mimic the two artists. The Presley complaint invokes Tennessee's Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer's voice. The Verge reports the suits closely mirror one Jason Isbell and others filed in September, which claimed Suno imitated them without claiming copyright infringement directly. Suno also faces suits from Sony, UMG and Reservoir. Suno says it blocks prompts naming artists and screens uploaded audio and lyrics.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): The Presley suit rests on a Tennessee law that treats a singer's voice as a right the estate can enforce apart from any copyright in the songs, and a win could give an artist's voice its own licensing price.
The Facts
  • Plaintiffs: a group of rights holders of Elvis Presley's music; the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records (publisher not named in the readable portion).
  • Claim: Suno illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The Presley suit claims a violation of Tennessee's ELVIS Act (Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security), which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer's voice.
  • Presley complaint: "Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists' identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of cold hard cash." Also: "Suno's ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect."
  • Precedent: Jason Isbell and others sued in September, claiming imitation but not copyright infringement directly (Variety reported Suno's motion to dismiss the Isbell suit, arguing there is "nothing unlawful" about invoking artist names to describe genres).
  • Other suits against Suno: Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir (The Verge).
  • Suno (spokesperson Cat McCormack): "Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone's name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist's work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists' names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse."

The Odyssey Carries a No-AI-Training Notice, and Nolan Says Only Studios Can Enforce It
Christopher Nolan, halfway through his first term as DGA president, said on the Hollywood Insiders podcast that the closing boilerplate of The Odyssey bars use of the film as AI training data.
Nolan said it is down to the studios to go after AI copies of films, because with very few exceptions directors do not hold the copyright in the films they make. He said he was very pleased that the end boilerplate of The Odyssey, Universal's release and his current Oscar contender, for the first time carries a message that the film cannot be ingested and used as training data. He argued that AI companies' fair-use defenses will not hold up in court long term, and said directors' residuals depend on how those copyrights are monetized.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Nolan's point is that a director's residuals ride on a copyright the studio owns, so whether a director's film ends up as AI training data is decided by the studio's enforcement, not by anything in the director's own contract.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Christopher Nolan, DGA president (elected September 2025; previously on the guild's Artificial Intelligence Committee). Venue: Hollywood Insiders podcast, reported by Deadline November 7, 2026.
  • On copyright: "With very few exceptions in the Guild, we are not the copyright holders of the films that we've worked on. It's down to the studios to do that."
  • On The Odyssey: "I was very pleased to see that the boilerplate at the end of The Odyssey, for the first time, it contains a message saying that this film cannot be ingested and used as training data."
  • On fair use: AI companies "hide behind fair-use provisions"; "longer term that won't hold up in court. There have already been some significant judgments against it."
  • On residuals (earlier Deadline interview): "our income, our residuals, depends on the appropriate monetization of those copyrights."
  • The Odyssey is a Universal release (Deadline: 52% of its $123.5 million opening came from IMAX and premium large-format screens).

Game Developers Can Now Hire Union Actors for Pitch Demos Before They Are Funded
SAG-AFTRA's Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement, introduced November 5, covers voice and motion work on game demos, vertical slices and prototypes made only to raise production money.
A project qualifies only if it has secured no more than 30% of its initial production funding, and the material cannot feel like a complete game, be sold or be shown publicly; projects that meet only some of those tests can seek a waiver. Hitmarker, reading the published contract, reports that crowdfunding pitches, milestone-funded projects and developers with publishing arrangements are excluded, that pitch session fees are freely negotiable, and that standard Interactive Media Agreement minimums and secondary payments apply if a performance is later used in the finished game.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): An actor on a pitch demo works under a union contract at a negotiated fee, and if the performance carries into the funded game the standard minimums and secondary payments follow it, though the agreement guarantees no role in the finished game.
The Facts
  • Agreement: Pre-Funding Pitch Interactive Media Agreement (SAG-AFTRA), announced November 5, 2026.
  • Covered material: demos, vertical slices, trailers, teasers, sizzle reels or playable prototypes "for the exclusive purpose of soliciting production funding for prospective projects."
  • Eligibility (SAG-AFTRA): no more than 30% of initial production funding secured; the material "must not provide the experience or impression of a complete interactive project"; not commercially released or publicly viewable or playable. Partial fits may seek a waiver via interactive@sagaftra.org.
  • Exclusions (Hitmarker, citing the published contract): crowdfunding pitches (waiver terms possible), projects seeking milestone funding, developers with existing publishing arrangements that provide production funding.
  • Pay (Hitmarker): pitch session fees freely negotiable between performer and developer; if the performance is later used in the finished game, the applicable Interactive Media Agreement terms, minimum session fees and secondary payments apply. No guarantee of employment on the eventual game.
  • Sean Astin, SAG-AFTRA president: the agreement "allows developers to up their game by bringing in professional voice and motion performance talent earlier in the process."
  • Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, national executive director: it "streamlines the hiring of professional union talent."

What Talent Needs to Know 6 opportunities · 6 challenges
Opportunities
  • The Duffers left Netflix for Paramount and still produce every Stranger Things spinoff because the franchise was carved out of their exclusivity, and that carve-out decides who keeps earning from the hit when a creator changes studios. (Project Economics)
  • Fable is selling a format where the performer supplies a face and a voice and the AI builds the rest, so the likeness license itself, how long it runs and where else it can be used, is the deal. (New Revenue Stream)
  • Foreign distributors who used to pay a minimum guarantee for one territory now want a stake in the IP and its merchandise, so a producer bringing an independent animated film to Lokia is negotiating who owns the consumer-products upside along with the presale price. (Rights Ownership)
  • Cramer built his paid club inside CNBC because the network's airtime does the marketing for him, and on-air talent with a loyal audience can now ask a network to build a subscription product around them and share in it. (New Revenue Stream)
  • With most film slots going to franchises and 3 Arts heading to full Lionsgate ownership, original filmmakers need a disciplined budget to get a slot, and 3 Arts clients should ask how conflicts are handled when their manager's owner is also the buyer. (Project Economics)
  • HBO is still a third bidder on high-end drama, and the first new package it buys outright under Skydance will show whether that budget holds, since the run of announcements so far was business closed before the merger.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • Fox now controls Tubi, the Roku Channel and the home screen in more than 100 million households, so a producer licensing a library to free ad-supported streaming has fewer separate buyers and one owner deciding what gets placed in front of viewers.
  • Studios are now pricing effects work on what AI saves, which makes approval over AI-generated shots one of the few places a director still controls how those savings change the picture.
  • Casting choices and release dates now carry a cash price before they are announced, so everyone on a production with advance knowledge, the talent's own team included, is part of a leak risk studios are now policing.
  • California scored the spinoff on the jobs it would add and gave no weight to two decades of Shondaland shows in Los Angeles, so Marinis, who also runs Grey's, runs two series in two states because of a credit decision she did not control.
  • Dumont got a 25-year-old script made by generating every performance himself, so an established director with a stalled project now has a way to finish it without a financier, and the actors who would have been cast are simply not in the budget.
  • Netflix is deciding whether to own a major Los Angeles lot at the same time it cancels leased stage space and shoots where subsidies are richer, so how much Netflix production stays in Los Angeles is still open.

Fox Now Owns Roku, the Front Door to Netflix, YouTube and Disney+ in 100 Million Homes
Fox closed its $22 billion Roku purchase Friday, ahead of the expected 2027 date, and put Roku, Tubi and Fox One in one new division that targets about $400 million in cost savings.
Fox Corp. closed its acquisition of Roku, valued at $22 billion ($160 a share, about $14.2 billion in cash and the rest in Fox Class A stock), well before the expected 2027 timing. Roku founder Anthony Wood joins the Fox board and co-chairs a new Fox Digital Platforms division with Paul Cheesbrough, covering Roku, Tubi, Fox One and Red Seat Ventures. Fox pledged to keep Roku an open platform that does not favor Fox News or Fox One. Roku had $4.1 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, 49 percent from advertising and 40 percent from subscriptions.

The Facts

  • Structure: Anthony Wood (Roku founder and CEO) joins the Fox board and is co-chair of Fox Digital Platforms; Paul Cheesbrough is co-chair and CEO of the division. Division includes Roku, Tubi, Fox One, Red Seat Ventures.

Studios Now Tell VFX Houses to Bring an AI Plan or Not Bid
Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah said studio legal departments barred generative AI early last year, and since this year's third quarter clients have told vendors, "If you don't have an AI strategy, don't bother."
Weta FX, the effects house behind Avatar and The Lord of the Rings, signed a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency and has worked with Taiwan's Moonshine Studio on generative AI for about six months. Seah said his clients, mainly the four biggest studios and the streamers, moved from a ban to allowing AI with pre-approval by mid-2025 to asking for an AI strategy, mostly to learn how much money it saves. Chief technology officer Kimball Thurston said Weta uses ByteDance's Seedance and Kling where clients permit, hosted outside China. Seah said Weta does not plan to replace artists.
Potential Talent Implication: Studios are now pricing effects work on what AI saves, which makes approval over AI-generated shots one of the few places a director still controls how those savings change the picture.
The Facts
  • Speaker: Daniel Seah, CEO, Weta FX; press briefing in Taipei after a partnership with the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) at Taiwan Creative Content Fest.
  • Client sequence (Seah): early 2025, memos from studio legal departments barring generative AI on their work; mid-2025, several clients allowed it with pre-approval and a small number of approved companies; around the turn of the year, clients asked about Weta's AI strategy, mostly for savings; since Q3 2026: "If you don't have an AI strategy, don't bother to work with us."
  • Moonshine Studio (Taiwan animation and VFX): Weta has worked with it for about six months. Screen International headline (body not read): Weta FX will build an AI hub in Taiwan and buy into Moonshine Studio.
  • Tools: Weta builds its own models; uses Kling AI and ByteDance's Seedance where clients permit, hosted outside China (Thurston: "You kind of have to").
  • TAICCA chair Sue Wang called it the biggest deal Taiwan has struck in the content industry. Taiwan's Ministry of Culture will introduce young talent to Weta; possible internships in Wellington, Melbourne, Vancouver.
  • Weta runs an open-source project, the Rongotai Model Train Club, that writes model training and dataset use into image metadata.
  • Thurston: "People still want to see the big star performing."

Twelve Foreign Distributors Pooled Into Lokia to Own the IP, Not Just Buy Territories
Distributors including Wild Bunch Germany, Kazoo Films and Noori Pictures formed Lokia, a Luxembourg company that will develop, finance and license films together as international presales decline.
Distributors from 12 territories formed Lokia ahead of the American Film Market, Deadline reported. Partners keep buying separately for their own markets but plan to develop and produce together, share revenue forecasts, invest in the IP and later acquire as a group. Founder Michael Favelle of Odin's Eye said licensing campaigns for independent animated films are not realistic without worldwide theatrical guarantees before financing. Former Marvel licensing executive Russell Brown is in talks with toy, game and publishing partners, with announcements expected in the fourth quarter. Fintage House will manage collection accounts.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Foreign distributors who used to pay a minimum guarantee for one territory now want a stake in the IP and its merchandise, so a producer bringing an independent animated film to Lokia is negotiating who owns the consumer-products upside along with the presale price.
The Facts
  • Lokia: incorporated in Luxembourg; distribution network of buyers from 12 territories, announced November 6, 2026, before AFM.
  • Partners: Wild Bunch Germany and Wild Bunch Austria; Praesens-Film (Switzerland); PRIS Audiovisuals (Portugal); Feelgood Entertainment (Greece); Kazoo Films (UK and Ireland); Noori Pictures (South Korea, Thailand, Vietnam); Filmhouse (Israel); Blitz Group (former Yugoslavia); Donart Film (Czech Republic); Mars Production (Turkey); Horizon Distribution (global airlines and shipping).
  • Plan: develop and produce together, pool market intelligence, pursue licensing and merchandising, later acquire as one entity; partners remain standalone financial entities and keep acquiring individually.
  • Deadline: "a direct response to consolidation in the market and the challenge posed by the declining international pre-sales model."
  • Principals: Michael Favelle (Odin's Eye Entertainment, chief creative officer and president of distribution); Heiko Nemmert (formerly Baby Giant, COO and president of production); Russell Brown (former Marvel Enterprises EVP of worldwide licensing, chief capital and monetisation officer).
  • Lokia OS: partners submit projects, distributors return revenue forecasts, financing and licensing partners see the aggregated picture before capital is committed.
  • Fintage House oversees reporting and collection accounts; co-chairman Robbert Aarts joins the board. Licensing partner announcements expected Q4 2026.
  • Prior groupings cited: Vuelta (2023); foreign distributors financing MadRiver films (2024); producers alliance The Creatives.

Studios Are Banning Employees From Betting on Casting and Release Dates
Studios and production companies have issued guidelines barring staff from prediction-market bets on earnings, casting and release dates, and one company set up an anonymous hotline to report colleagues.
The Hollywood Reporter learned that studios and production companies are quietly telling employees not to bet on prediction markets about studio earnings, casting or release dates, or to pass information to others who bet. PMC, which owns THR, Variety, Deadline and Dick Clark Productions, banned bets on award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates. BetOnline pulled its James Bond casting market this week after money moved sharply to Callum Turner. Betting on box office receipts is already illegal under the 1958 Onion Futures Act.
Potential Talent Implication: Casting choices and release dates now carry a cash price before they are announced, so everyone on a production with advance knowledge, the talent's own team included, is part of a leak risk studios are now policing.
The Facts
  • Studio guidelines (unnamed companies): no prediction-market bets on studio earnings, casting or release dates; no tipping friends or family; at least one company has an anonymous reporting hotline.
  • PMC handbook update (recent weeks): bans betting on "award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates."
  • Kalshi disclosed in February that a MrBeast video editor made $5,000 betting on confidential MrBeast content; fired and fined $20,000.
  • BetOnline temporarily pulled its James Bond casting market after "sharp money" moved Callum Turner above Jack Lowden.
  • Mitts and Ofir study (March): an estimated $143 million in anomalous profit on Polymarket over two years.
  • CFTC view: award-show bets (Oscars, Emmys) allowed as contests; game shows and reality competitions unresolved.
  • Onion Futures Act of 1958 bans only onion futures and motion picture box office receipts.
  • Joshua Mitts, Columbia Law: entertainment markets have "a high degree of asymmetric information" and "very little social utility."

Bruno Dumont Made His Next Feature With Generative AI and No Actors After French Financing Dried Up
The two-time Cannes Grand Prix winner wrapped The End, an English-language sci-fi thriller, generating its images, performances and sound himself from his Paris home, and plans festivals and a 2027 theatrical release.
Bruno Dumont told Screen International his feature The End was made entirely with generative AI, without actors or a film crew, on what Screen calls a shoestring budget. He wrote the script more than 25 years ago and shelved it because its earthquake and asteroid sequences were too expensive to shoot. He began in August and has wrapped. The Facts
  • Director: Bruno Dumont (Cannes Grand Prix for Humanity, 1999, and Flanders, 2006; Berlinale Silver Bear jury prize for The Empire, 2024; Red Rocks premiered in Cannes Directors' Fortnight 2026).

  • Method: generative AI for images, performances and sound, made from his Paris home; no actors, no traditional crew. Works scene by scene from his own shot breakdowns; used faces from Flemish paintings as references for characters.

  • Business: producing independently; no sales agent attached.

  • Context, same week (Screen International, Jeremy Kay, AFM preview): AGC Studios will screen Gods Don't Give Gifts, an AI-rendered animation from YouTuber Zack London (Gossip Goblin), to AFM buyers on the market's first day.

2026-11-05 Thursday 14 stories

What Talent Needs to Know 10 opportunities · 4 challenges
Opportunities
  • A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license. (Rights Ownership)
  • When one format brings in close to a third of a film's gross, the director who shoots for it is delivering a revenue line, which can give IMAX screen commitments and format exclusivity real weight in a filmmaker's deal. (Project Economics)
  • A single Spider-Man release moved Sony Pictures' quarterly profit more than sixfold, a figure that may carry weight for anyone negotiating on the next Spider-Man film, since the studio's reliance on the franchise is now in its own results. (Project Economics)
  • Sony's record is a film and franchise story while its TV production business shrank, so the open doors at Sony are franchise film and the new anime and live-action adaptation lane, not a bigger TV budget. (Project Economics)
  • With the largest exhibitor healthy and premium screens carrying a third of US admissions, filmmakers who shoot for large formats and filmmakers at Netflix have stronger grounds to ask for premium-screen commitments, full windows and box office bonuses. (Project Economics)
  • When IMAX screens carry nearly a third of a film's gross and streamers buy IMAX-only theatrical runs, an IMAX commitment becomes a deal term worth negotiating, from camera and budget to IMAX weeks and release-date protection. (Project Economics)
  • A horror filmmaker managed by Maxwell or Rowbotham now has a manager who also runs a Lionsgate buyer, so where a project is set up, and on what terms, may need to be shopped against other buyers before Render Road is the answer.
  • Lionsgate now builds its slate on properties it can repeat across film, stage, tours and games, so talent attached to a Lionsgate franchise is attached to more than one revenue line, and the participation terms decide which of those lines it shares in. (New Revenue Stream)
  • A home release no longer ends a big film's theatrical life, so a filmmaker's re-release terms, from format screens to how a second run's grosses count toward box office bonuses, are now worth writing into the deal. (Project Economics)
  • Letterboxd's 30 million monthly users and their ratings would sit with a news publisher rather than a studio, which keeps the largest film word-of-mouth platform outside any one distributor's control.
Challenges & Headwinds
  • With three animation labels under one owner and the Netflix order gone, the label a filmmaker's deal sits at, and the turnaround rights in it, may decide whether a project in development keeps a home.
  • When a buyer treats the theatrical run as marketing for its streaming service, the box office number that usually sets bonuses and backend no longer measures what the film earned the buyer, so the streaming performance terms carry the real value.
  • Because A24 sells foreign rights territory by territory, the overseas gross on an A24 hit mostly stays with regional distributors, which may cap what a filmmaker's backend can draw from it, and a sale would put those deals in a new owner's hands.
  • When one of the town's leading deal lawyers says studio films under $70 million lose money unless they are horror, a mid-budget drama or comedy may need a horror-sized budget, a tentpole's scale or outside financing to get made at a studio.
The Cocaine Cowboys Directors Got Their Film Back From Netflix and Remade It With AI for $200,000
Billy Corben and Alfred Spellman spent about $200,000 using AI to rework nearly 4,000 shots of their 2006 documentary after Netflix's license reverted, and are raising $5 million for a YouTube-first studio.
Rakontur, the Miami company behind Cocaine Cowboys, made documentaries for Netflix, HBO and Hulu until those buyers cut nonfiction spending. Rights to the original film reverted from Netflix this year. Over eight months the directors rebuilt it with ByteDance's Seedance and Google's Veo; the new version premieres on YouTube Nov. 13, and Rakontur expects to recoup through licensing, sponsorships and companion programming rather than YouTube ads alone. Rakontur Direct, with former Complex Networks CEO Rich Antoniello, targets 260 releases a year by its second year and will license shows to streamers only after they premiere on its own channels.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A documentary whose license reverts can now be rebuilt for a fraction of its original cost and sold again, which makes the reversion date and the right to make new versions of the film two of the most valuable terms in a nonfiction license.
The Facts
  • Filmmakers: Billy Corben and Alfred Spellman, Rakontur (Miami), 25 years in business; credits for Netflix (Cocaine Cowboys: The Kings of Miami, 2021), HBO (537 Votes), Hulu (God Forbid), Neon (Men of War), MSNBC Films (From Russia with Lev, Emmy-nominated).
  • Rights: Cocaine Cowboys (2006), licensed to Netflix, reverted to Rakontur in 2026.
  • Remake: roughly $200,000; nearly 4,000 shots revisited; eight months; tools: ByteDance Seedance, Google Veo, Topaz for interview footage. YouTube premiere Nov. 13, six days before Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • Recoup plan (Spellman): licensing, sponsorships and related programming, not YouTube ad revenue alone.
  • Rakontur Direct: seeking $5 million from strategic partners for about two years of operation; target 260 releases a year (about five a week) by year two; initial slate short-form, episodes of 15 minutes or less; first series A Sunny Place for Shady People; streamer licensing only after premiere on Rakontur's channels.
  • Hire: Rich Antoniello, co-founder and former CEO of Complex Networks (sold to BuzzFeed for $300 million in 2021).
  • Spellman: Rakontur Direct is "a nonfiction media company that produces original programming, publishes directly to audiences and owns the resulting intellectual property."
  • Spellman: "AI is the third revolution we've lived through in this business."

Amazon Sends Most of Its Theatrical Films to Prime Video 47 Days After Opening
